prohibited_recommendations: Do not give benzodiazepines or other sedatives for agitation or sleep: they precipitate and prolong hepatic encephalopathy; manage agitation with reorientation, a safe environment and treatment of the precipitant (EASL 2022).
Do not prescribe opioids, which worsen HE; for pain use acetaminophen up to 2 g per day.
Do not use trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole for treatment or prophylaxis: documented sulfa anaphylaxis.
required_recommendations: Treat SBP with IV ceftriaxone 2 g daily (or cefotaxime), adjusted to culture, plus albumin 1.5 g/kg on day 1 and 1 g/kg on day 3; repeat paracentesis at 48 hours if there is no clinical improvement (EASL 2018). The sulfa allergy does not contraindicate cephalosporins.
Blood, urine and ascitic cultures are drawn before the first antibiotic dose, which is not delayed for them.

Lactulose 25 mL every 1-2 hours until at least two soft bowel movements, then titrated to 2-3 soft bowel movements per day (ACG 2026 recommendation 10; EASL 2022); avoid over-titration, which causes dehydration, hypokalemia and kidney injury.
Continue rifaximin 550 mg twice daily with lactulose for this recurrent overt episode (ACG 2026; EASL 2022).
Monitor creatinine daily; reduce or hold carvedilol if systolic BP falls below 90 mmHg or kidney injury develops (Baveno VII).
After this episode, give long-term SBP prophylaxis with norfloxacin or ciprofloxacin; never trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole (sulfa anaphylaxis) (EASL 2018).
Review omeprazole and stop it unless there is a specific indication: proton pump inhibitors are associated with SBP and HE in cirrhosis (EASL 2022).
Inform the transplant team: overt HE with SBP in a listed patient with HCC, MELD-Na 28; listing is reviewed once the infection is controlled.

avoided_actions.rationale: No clinical suspicion for hepatopulmonary syndrome, portopulmonary hypertension, or endocarditis; echocardiography is not part of the HE workup.
Amyloid PET has no role in HE workup; reversible metabolic encephalopathy is the issue, not Alzheimer pathology.
DaTscan has no role in HE workup; the question is metabolic encephalopathy, not nigrostriatal degeneration.
Early-onset AD genetic panel has no role in HE workup; reversible metabolic encephalopathy is the diagnosis under consideration.

accepted: Hepatic encephalopathy (West Haven grade III), hepatitis C cirrhosis with small HCC on transplant list (Child-Pugh C, MELD-Na 28), precipitated by spontaneous bacterial peritonitis

differential.key_features: MRI if clinical course atypical or focal deficits develop.

key_clinical_evidence: Child-Pugh C (14: bilirubin 4.6 3, albumin 2.4 3, INR 2.1 2, moderate ascites 3, HE grade 3 3); MELD-Na 28 (creatinine 1.6, bilirubin 4.6, INR 2.1, sodium 131)

HE is a clinical diagnosis: West Haven grading, evidence of liver dysfunction and exclusion of other causes of altered mental status; ammonia is supportive only and correlates poorly with grade (ACG 2026; EASL 2022).

Precipitant identification is more actionable than the ammonia number: infection (SBP especially), GI bleed, electrolyte disturbance (hypokalemia/hyponatremia), constipation, sedative/CNS-depressant use, dehydration, dietary protein load, renal failure.
Documented overt HE episodes affect transplant prioritization decisions and should be communicated to the transplant team.

An elevated ammonia neither grades nor confirms hepatic encephalopathy and repeat levels are not used to guide treatment; a normal ammonia in a confused patient with cirrhosis should prompt a search for another cause (ACG 2026 recommendation 5 and key concept 14; EASL 2022).

patient.history_present_illness: A 63-year-old man with known hepatitis C cirrhosis and hepatocellular carcinoma on the liver transplant waiting list was brought to the emergency department by his wife due to three days of progressively worsening confusion. His wife reports that he initially seemed forgetful and was mixing up family members' names, which she attributed to fatigue. By day two, he was sleeping most of the day, becoming difficult to rouse for meals, and had stopped taking his afternoon lactulose dose because he kept forgetting. On the day of presentation, he could not recognize their home and was asking to go back to Mexico (he has lived in the United States for 35 years). He had no witnessed seizures, no falls, no headaches, and no complaints of pain. His wife noted his abdomen appeared more distended than usual and that his urine had been darker over the past two days. She also reported that he had developed a low-grade fever at home (measured 38.2°C) and had complained of mild abdominal discomfort. He has been compliant with his transplant evaluation requirements and had a routine hepatology appointment scheduled for next week. He has been abstinent from alcohol for 8 years and achieved sustained virologic response on hepatitis C treatment. His wife denied any recent medication changes, new supplements, or obvious dietary indiscretions. He had a prior episode of hepatic encephalopathy eighteen months ago that required hospitalization but resolved completely with lactulose and rifaximin intensification.

neurological_exam.additional: Scleral icterus present. Mild jaundice. Moderate abdominal distension with shifting dullness consistent with ascites. No spider angiomata prominent. Mild palmar erythema. No fetor hepaticus appreciated on this presentation.

neurological_exam.mental_status: GCS 10 (E3V3M4). Disoriented to time and place; knows his name. Somnolent but arousable with verbal stimuli. Answers questions with single words or short phrases, most inappropriate. Asterixis present bilaterally. Number connection test performance markedly impaired — unable to complete.
neurological_exam.motor: Moves all four extremities spontaneously. Decreased tone in upper and lower extremities. No focal weakness appreciated.
neurological_exam.reflexes: DTRs 2+ at biceps, triceps; 1+ patellar bilaterally. No Babinski sign.
neurological_exam.sensory: Limited cooperation; withdraws to painful stimuli symmetrically.
